# Sensitivity and identifiability

Sensitivity analysis asks how much a chosen model output changes when an input
changes. Identifiability asks a different question: can the data, in principle,
distinguish the parameters or only a combination of them? Keeping those
questions separate prevents a common mistake in epidemic modeling: treating a
precise numerical estimate as evidence that every biological parameter is
learnable.

## Learning goals

By the end of this chapter you should be able to:

- distinguish local, global, and structural identifiability analyses;
- compute local state sensitivities with the current
  [SciMLSensitivity.jl API](https://docs.sciml.ai/SciMLSensitivity/stable/);
- use a small Sobol analysis with
  [GlobalSensitivity.jl](https://docs.sciml.ai/GlobalSensitivity/stable/);
- use [StructuralIdentifiability.jl](https://docs.sciml.ai/StructuralIdentifiability/stable/)
  to expose a parameter combination that observations cannot separate; and
- validate a sensitivity calculation against conservation and a finite
  perturbation.

## Model assumptions and classification

We use the homogeneous SIR model from @kermack1927. It is a deterministic,
continuous-time, continuous-state, population model. Individuals move
irreversibly from susceptible to infectious to removed; the population is
closed, well mixed, and has frequency-dependent transmission. The contact
rate and per-contact transmission probability are kept as separate inputs even
though the ODE depends on their product.

With $S(0)=990$, $I(0)=10$, $R(0)=0$, $N=1000$, contact rate
$c=10$, transmission probability $\beta=0.05$, and recovery rate
$\gamma=0.25$, the initial effective reproduction number is
$\mathcal{R}_0=\beta c/\gamma=2$. These values are the course baseline.

## Equations

Let $x(t)=(S(t),I(t),R(t))$. The transition rates are
$q_{\mathrm{inf}}=\beta cSI/N$ and $q_{\mathrm{rec}}=\gamma I$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\mathrm dS}{\mathrm dt} &= -q_{\mathrm{inf}},\\
\frac{\mathrm dI}{\mathrm dt} &= q_{\mathrm{inf}}-q_{\mathrm{rec}},\\
\frac{\mathrm dR}{\mathrm dt} &= q_{\mathrm{rec}}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-sensitivity-sir}

The local sensitivity matrix is
$J_x(t)=\partial x(t)/\partial\theta$, where
$\theta=(\beta,c,\gamma)$. If a scalar quantity of interest is
$z=h(x(t),\theta)$, then a first-order perturbation is
$\Delta z\approx \nabla_\theta z\,\Delta\theta$. This approximation is
local: it is informative near one parameter vector, not across an entire
plausible range.

Structural identifiability is about the observation map, not the solver. If
only incidence $y=\beta cSI/N$ is observed, the transformation
$(\beta,c)\mapsto(a\beta,c/a)$ leaves the transmission term unchanged.
Therefore $\beta$ and $c$ cannot be separated without additional information
or an informative design.

## Julia implementation

The course module provides the baseline constructors and plotting theme. The
right-hand side below is written out as a pedagogical three-parameter kernel so
that the derivative in @eq-sensitivity-sir is visible in the code.

```{julia}
using CairoMakie
using GlobalSensitivity
using ModelingToolkit
using OrdinaryDiffEq
using SciMLSensitivity
using StructuralIdentifiability

course_root = normpath(joinpath(@__DIR__, ".."))
include(joinpath(course_root, "src", "EpiModelingCourse.jl"))
using .EpiModelingCourse

baseline = BASELINE_PARAMETERS
u0 = Float64[
    BASELINE_INITIAL_STATE.S,
    BASELINE_INITIAL_STATE.I,
    BASELINE_INITIAL_STATE.R,
]
N = baseline.N
p0 = [baseline.beta, baseline.contact_rate, baseline.gamma]
tgrid = collect(0.0:1.0:40.0)

function sir_kernel!(du, u, p, t)
    β, c, γ = p
    S, I, R = u
    incidence = β * c * S * I / N
    du[1] = -incidence
    du[2] = incidence - γ * I
    du[3] = γ * I
    return nothing
end
```

### Local sensitivities

`ODEForwardSensitivityProblem` augments the original ODE with the variational
equations. `extract_local_sensitivities` returns the state trajectory and a
Jacobian for each saved time. This is the forward-sensitivity route in
SciMLSensitivity; adjoint methods are preferable when there are many
parameters but only a few scalar outputs.

```{julia}
local_problem = ODEForwardSensitivityProblem(
    sir_kernel!,
    u0,
    (first(tgrid), last(tgrid)),
    p0,
)
local_solution = solve(
    local_problem,
    Tsit5();
    saveat = tgrid,
    abstol = 1e-9,
    reltol = 1e-9,
)
local_states, local_jacobians = extract_local_sensitivities(
    local_solution,
    true,
)
final_jacobian = local_jacobians[end]
final_jacobian
```

The rows of `final_jacobian` correspond to $S$, $I$, and $R$, and its columns
correspond to $\beta$, $c$, and $\gamma$. The following figure displays the
infectious-row sensitivities through time.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ch10-local-sensitivity
#| fig-cap: "Local derivatives of the infectious state with respect to the three SIR inputs."
fig = Figure(size = (800, 450))
ax = Axis(
    fig[1, 1],
    xlabel = "time",
    ylabel = "∂I/∂parameter",
    title = "Local forward sensitivities",
)
parameter_labels = ["β", "c", "γ"]
parameter_colors = [:steelblue, :darkorange, :seagreen]
for j in 1:3
    lines!(
        ax,
        tgrid,
        [jacobian[2, j] for jacobian in local_jacobians],
        label = parameter_labels[j],
        color = parameter_colors[j],
    )
end
axislegend(ax)
fig
```

### Global sensitivity

Local derivatives can miss interactions and changes in ranking away from
$p_0$. GlobalSensitivity evaluates a scalar output over a specified parameter
box. Here the output is the peak infectious population. `samples=32` keeps
the example short; a production analysis needs a convergence study over
larger designs and, ideally, uncertainty distributions justified by data.

```{julia}
function peak_infectious(p)
    problem = ODEProblem(sir_kernel!, u0, (0.0, 40.0), Float64.(p))
    solution = solve(problem, Tsit5(); saveat = 1.0, abstol = 1e-8, reltol = 1e-8)
    return maximum(Array(solution)[2, :])
end

parameter_bounds = [
    [0.02, 0.08],  # β
    [5.0, 15.0],   # c
    [0.15, 0.40],  # γ
]
sobol = gsa(peak_infectious, Sobol(), parameter_bounds; samples = 32)
sobol_first = sobol.S1
sobol_total = sobol.ST
sobol_first, sobol_total
```

`S1` measures the first-order contribution and `ST` includes interactions.
The plot is a compact way to compare the two summaries rather than treating
one ranking as universal.

```{julia}
#| label: fig-ch10-global-sensitivity
#| fig-cap: "First-order and total Sobol indices for the infectious peak."
fig = Figure(size = (800, 450))
ax = Axis(
    fig[1, 1],
    xticks = (1:3, ["β", "c", "γ"]),
    ylabel = "Sobol index",
    title = "Global sensitivity of the peak",
)
barplot!(ax, 1:3, sobol_first, dodge = fill(1, 3), color = :steelblue)
barplot!(ax, (1:3) .+ 0.35, sobol_total, dodge = fill(1, 3), color = :darkorange)
Legend(fig[1, 2], [PolyElement(color = :steelblue), PolyElement(color = :darkorange)],
    ["first order", "total"])
fig
```

### Structural identifiability

StructuralIdentifiability uses symbolic differential algebra. We deliberately
omit the known population scale in this small example to highlight the
confounding of $\beta$ and $c$ in a mass-action-style observation. The package
uses ASCII parameter names in this interface, so `b` and `c` stand for
$\beta$ and $c$.

```{julia}
@parameters b c g
@independent_variables t
@variables S(t) I(t) R(t) y(t)
D = Differential(t)
identifiability_system = ODESystem(
    [
        D(S) ~ -b * c * S * I,
        D(I) ~ b * c * S * I - g * I,
        D(R) ~ g * I,
    ],
    t;
    name = :SIRIdentifiability,
)
identifiability = assess_identifiability(
    identifiability_system;
    measured_quantities = [y ~ b * c * S * I],
    funcs_to_check = [b, c, g, b * c],
)
identifiability
```

The expected interpretation is that `b` and `c` are nonidentifiable while
`b*c` and `g` are identifiable for this observation choice. Adding an
independent observation, fixing the contact rate from external information,
or collecting contact-pattern data changes the identification problem; no
optimizer can recover information absent from the observation map.

## Validation

The forward sensitivity solve should conserve total population, and its
finite perturbation should agree with the derivative at the scale of the
chosen perturbation. The checks below are deliberately numerical rather than
asserting a particular rounded sensitivity value.

```{julia}
population_error = maximum(abs.(vec(sum(local_states; dims = 1)) .- N))

ε = 1e-5
perturbed = copy(p0)
perturbed[1] += ε
perturbed_solution = solve(
    ODEProblem(sir_kernel!, u0, (0.0, 40.0), perturbed),
    Tsit5();
    saveat = tgrid,
    abstol = 1e-9,
    reltol = 1e-9,
)
finite_difference = (Array(perturbed_solution)[2, end] - local_states[2, end]) / ε
sensitivity_difference = abs(finite_difference - final_jacobian[2, 1])
sensitivity_relative_difference =
    sensitivity_difference / (1 + abs(final_jacobian[2, 1]))

@assert population_error < 1e-6
@assert sensitivity_relative_difference < 1e-3
(population_error = population_error, sensitivity_difference = sensitivity_difference,
    sensitivity_relative_difference = sensitivity_relative_difference)
```

## Interpretation and limitations

The local plot describes a neighborhood of the baseline; it is not a
probability distribution or a causal effect. The Sobol result is conditional
on the rectangular bounds and the small quasi-random design. Structural
identifiability is an idealized, noiseless, continuous-observation result,
whereas practical identifiability also depends on observation times,
measurement error, initial conditions, and model misspecification. In
particular, a fit of $\beta c$ does not justify separate biological claims
about $\beta$ and $c$. The SciMLSensitivity, GlobalSensitivity, and
StructuralIdentifiability APIs used here are documented in their current
official links above; the computations intentionally remain small enough to
inspect and rerun.

## Exercises

### Exercise 1 {#ch10-ex1}

Change `peak_infectious` to return the final removed count instead of the
infectious peak. Re-run the Sobol calculation with the same bounds, compare
the first-order and total indices, and explain why the ranking can differ
between a transient output and a cumulative output.

### Exercise 2 {#ch10-ex2}

Extend `identifiability_system` with an observable `n(t) ~ S + I + R`.
Assess `[b, c, g, b*c]` again. State which confounding remains, if any, and
describe one additional data stream that would make the separate contact rate
credible.
